title: Aging Report: Meaning & Role in Accounts Receivable (AR)
summary: Learn how an accounts receivable aging report helps you track outstanding invoices and prioritize collections to improve cash flow.
body_markdown:
An accounts receivable aging report lists every unpaid customer invoice, grouped by how long it’s been outstanding: usually current, 1 to 30, 31 to 60, 61 to 90 and over 90 days past due. Finance teams use it to see who to chase first, spot customers at risk and estimate how much they might never collect.


Reviewed every week or month, it’s one of the simplest ways to protect cash flow. In this guide, you’ll learn:

## What is an accounts receivable (AR) aging report?


An accounts receivable aging report, often called an AR aging report or simply an aging report, lists every unpaid customer invoice and groups it by how long it has been outstanding. It shows at a glance who owes you money, how much and how late they are.


Most aging reports sort invoices into these buckets:


- **Current:** not yet due
- **1 to 30 days past due**
- **31 to 60 days past due**
- **61 to 90 days past due**
- **Over 90 days past due**


For each customer, the report shows the total of their[outstanding invoices](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-collections/outstanding-invoices) in each bucket, along with the overall balance. Many teams also show the invoice numbers, amounts and due dates behind each figure.


Most B2B finance teams age invoices from the **due date** , so an invoice only counts as late once its payment terms have passed. Some businesses age from the invoice date instead, which shows how long the money has been owed in total. Either works, as long as you use the same method every time so your reports stay comparable.


Finance teams use the aging report to decide which customers to chase first, to spot[past-due invoices](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-collections/past-due-invoices) before they turn into write-offs, and to estimate how much of their receivables they may never collect. In simple terms, it tells you who owes you money and how late they are.


## What does an AR aging report look like?


An aging report is a table, with one row per customer and one column per aging bucket. Here’s a simple example for a company with $62,000 in outstanding receivables:


Here’s the same report as a table:


Customer Current 1–30 days 31–60 days 61–90 days 90+ days Total


Acme Corp $12,000 $4,000 – – – $16,000


Brightline Ltd $8,500 – $3,200 – – $11,700


Cobalt Systems – $6,000 $2,500 $1,800 – $10,300


Delta Health $15,000 $2,000 – – – $17,000


Evergreen Media – – – $2,200 $4,800 $7,000


Total $35,500 $12,000 $5,700 $4,000 $4,800 $62,000


% of total 57% 19% 9% 7% 8% 100%


Reading across a row shows how a single customer is paying. Reading down a column shows how much of your receivables sits in each stage of lateness. The bottom row is the quickest health check: in this example, 57% of receivables are current, and 43% are past due, with 15% more than 60 days late.


Some patterns stand out straight away. Acme Corp and Delta Health are mostly current, with small amounts just past due. Cobalt Systems has balances spread across three overdue buckets, which suggests its payments are slipping. Evergreen Media has nothing current at all, and most of its balance is over 90 days late, so it’s the account to look at first.


### Aging summary vs aging detail report


Most accounting systems offer two versions of the aging report:


Aging summary report Aging detail report


What it shows One row per customer, with totals for each bucket One row per invoice, with invoice number, dates, amount and days past due


Best for A quick overview of AR health and month-end reporting Day-to-day collections work and following up on specific invoices


Typical users CFOs, controllers and leadership AR specialists and collectors


The summary tells you where the problem is, and the detail tells you what to do about it. Most teams review the summary weekly or monthly, often alongside their[AR dashboard](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-metrics/ar-dashboard) , and work from the detail report when they’re chasing payments.


## How do you create an aging report?


To create an aging report, list every unpaid invoice, work out how many days each one is past due, sort them into aging buckets, then total the buckets for each customer. Most accounting systems do this automatically, but the logic is the same whether you use software or a spreadsheet.


### How to create an aging report, step by step


**Step 1: Gather all open invoices.** Pull a list of every unpaid invoice, with the customer name, invoice number, invoice date, due date and amount still owed.


**Step 2: Calculate days past due.** For each invoice, subtract the due date from today’s date. A negative or zero result means the invoice isn’t due yet.


**Step 3: Assign each invoice to an aging bucket.** Place each invoice in Current, 1 to 30, 31 to 60, 61 to 90 or 90+ days past due, based on the result from step 2.


**Step 4: Group by customer and total each bucket.** Add up the amounts in each bucket for every customer, then calculate the totals and the percentage of receivables in each bucket.


**Step 5: Prioritize overdue accounts.** Start with the oldest and largest balances, since they carry the highest risk of becoming[bad debt](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-metrics/bad-debt-calculation) , and check whether any customer is slipping into later buckets over time.


### Building an aging report in Excel or your ERP


**In Excel or Google Sheets,** export your open invoices with the columns from step 1, then add two calculated columns:


- **Days past due:** =TODAY()-D2, where D2 is the due date
- **Aging bucket:** =IF(E2<=0,”Current”,IF(E2<=30,”1-30″,IF(E2<=60,”31-60″,IF(E2<=90,”61-90″,”90+”)))), where E2 is days past due


Then create a pivot table with customers as rows, aging buckets as columns, and the sum of the open amount as values. That gives you the same layout as the sample report above. The drawback is that the report is only as current as your last export, so it needs rebuilding every time you review it.


If you’d rather start from a ready-made version, our free AR aging report template has the formulas and buckets already set up.


**In your accounting system or ERP,** the report is usually built in. NetSuite, Sage Intacct, QuickBooks and Xero all include standard aging reports for accounts receivable, typically in both a summary and a detail version. QuickBooks and Xero call them “A/R Aging” and “Aged Receivables” reports respectively. These pull directly from your ledger, so they’re accurate as of the moment you run them, but they show balances rather than the follow-up history or context behind each overdue invoice.


## Why is an AR aging report important?


An AR aging report shows where your cash is stuck and how long it’s been stuck there. That makes it one of the most useful tools for protecting cash flow, prioritizing collections and keeping bad debt under control.


Late payment is common in B2B. According to the[2026 Atradius Payment Practices Barometer](https://group.atradius.com/knowledge-and-research/news/a-complex-payment-risk-landscape-emerges-for-north-american-businesses) for North America, late payments affect seven in ten companies, and overdue invoices make up an average of 23% of B2B receivables. Most of those invoices are paid within a month of the due date, which is exactly why it matters to catch the ones that aren’t before they age further.


Without an aging report, it’s hard to track unpaid invoices accurately, which leads to missed follow-ups, poor visibility into[cash flow](https://upflow.io/blog/cfo-reads/cash-flow-analysis) and inaccurate assumptions in your forecasts. At a high level, an aging report helps you:


- Keep visibility into your receivables[timeline](https://www.visme.co/timeline-maker/)
- Prioritize collection efforts by urgency
- Act on late payments early instead of reacting to them
- Reduce the risk of cash flow disruptions


Reviewed regularly, it helps you make better decisions about collections, credit policies and[customer relationships](https://upflow.io/financial-relationship-management) before small delays become big problems.


### 1. Estimate bad debt risk


Some invoices go so far past their due date that they can’t be collected and have to be written off as bad debt. The[IRS](https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p334.pdf) lets businesses deduct bad debts, but only once they’ve determined the debt is worthless.


The aging report gives you the data to estimate those losses each period, using the aging method described above, and to calculate your[bad debt expense](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-metrics/bad-debt-calculation) accurately. It also shows you where to review your policies. For example, if one customer keeps contributing to bad debt, you may need to tighten their credit terms.


As a rule, the longer an invoice goes unpaid, the less likely you are to collect it. Reviewing the aging report regularly keeps bad debt under control.


### 2. Spot cash flow problems early


Healthy cash flow depends on customers paying on time. The[U.S. Chamber of Commerce](https://www.uschamber.com/co/start/strategy/why-small-businesses-fail) lists cash flow problems as the first reason small businesses fail, and even profitable companies can run short of cash when large invoices are paid late.


Imagine a large order where you’ve paid suppliers upfront but the customer pays 60 days late. The gap has to be covered from your own cash or by borrowing, and the cost can wipe out the margin on the deal. The aging report makes these situations visible early, so you can follow up, adjust your forecast or arrange financing before cash gets tight.


Are late payments piling up? Our[free guide with tips to get paid on time](https://insights.upflow.io/en/wp-tips-get-paid) covers practical ways to tackle them.


### 3. Improve your collection practices


The aging report shows you whether your collection process is working. If several accounts regularly reach 60 to 90 days, your follow-up probably starts too late or isn’t consistent enough.


Sometimes the fix is simple: a customer’s internal payment cycle doesn’t match your invoice dates, so aligning the two reduces late payments. In other cases, you can[improve AR collection](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-collections/improve-accounts-receivable-collection) by prioritizing your efforts, sending reminders on the first day an invoice is late and adding more personal follow-up for key accounts. These[accounts receivable management best practices](https://upflow.io/blog/ar-collections/accounts-receivable-management) all start with knowing which invoices are late, which is exactly what the aging report shows.


### 4. Assess your credit policies


The aging report is also a quick way to test your credit policy. If most of your overdue balance comes from a single customer, the problem is likely with that account, and you need to find out why they’re paying late.


If many customers are falling behind, the issue is more likely your credit policy itself, such as terms that are too generous or credit extended to higher-risk customers. Comparing your aging profile over time, and against industry norms, shows whether your credit risk is under control.


## How do you automate an aging report?


You automate an aging report by connecting your accounting system or ERP to[accounts receivable software](https://upflow.io/accounts-receivable-software) that updates aging buckets automatically as invoices are issued and paid. Instead of exporting data and rebuilding a spreadsheet, you get a live view of what’s outstanding, so you can act on overdue invoices the day they slip into a new bucket.


A manual aging report is accurate only at the moment you build it. As soon as a customer pays or a new invoice goes out, the numbers are out of date, and finance teams end up chasing customers who have already paid or missing invoices that have just become overdue. Automation fixes that by keeping the aging data in sync with your ledger, and by linking the report to the actions that follow from it: reminders, escalations and follow-up tasks.


When you compare tools, look for an aging view that you can break down by customer, owner or segment, that shows how your aging profile has changed over time, and that lets you go straight from a bucket to the invoices behind it. Just as important is what happens next: the best tools use the same aging data to trigger collection workflows, so every overdue invoice gets the right follow-up without anyone building a to-do list by hand.
